    Challenge

    Challenge: read the pileup

    1. In the text view, count the reads that show C (or c) in column 21, and the reads that match the reference there. What genotype do you expect the caller to report for HG002?
    2. The benchmark says HG002 is homozygous for the ALT allele A at chr20:85,259 (reference G). Write the tview command that shows this site in column 21, and predict what you will see before you run it.

    1. Column 21 holds 39 reads: 14 show C or c and 25 match the reference T, and the consensus line shows Y. That is 36% C, fewer than half, but not unusual for a heterozygous site: with 39 reads, a perfectly balanced site gives 14 or fewer C reads 5.4% of the time, and 14 or fewer reads of either allele 10.8% of the time (binomial, Episode 1). Expect the caller to report 0/1. Episode 5A shows how the caller actually decides: it compares the likelihoods of the three genotypes rather than testing the balance. The benchmark for HG002 agrees: 0/1 at this position.

    2. Start 20 bases earlier, at 85,239:

      BASH 

      samtools tview -d T -i -w 41 -p chr20:85239 results/bam/HG002.markdup.bam ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa

      Nearly every read should show A or a in column 21, and the consensus line shows A: a homozygous ALT site. In the test run, all 50 reads in column 21 show A or a and none matches the reference G.

    Graphical viewing is decided in P6 (IGV through a graphical session, or prepared snapshots). Until then, samtools tview -d T is the locus view for this episode. Learners can also run samtools tview without -d T for the interactive viewer (? for help, q to quit).

    Base quality recalibration (concept only)

    Sequencers can be systematically over- or under-confident in their base qualities, for example in certain sequence contexts or late in a read. Base quality score recalibration (BQSR) in GATK models these errors from mismatches at positions that are not known variant sites, and rewrites the qualities (GATK documentation). It needs a database of known variants for the organism.

    We do not recalibrate in this workshop. bcftools does not require it, and many organisms have no database of known variants. GATK’s own pipeline uses it; Episode 5B, self-paced, discusses where it applies.

    Summary

    Key Points
    • bwa mem finds seeds with an index of the reference, extends them into local alignments, and soft-clips ends that do not match.
    • Mapping quality is the Phred-scaled probability that a read is placed wrongly; reads that fit several places equally well get MAPQ 0 and can create false variants.
    • Read groups label reads by sample; SM becomes the sample name in the VCF, so it must come from the sample sheet.
    • The order is bwa mem, samtools fixmate -m, samtools sort, samtools markdup; duplicates are flagged, not removed, and the caller skips them.
    • -K makes bwa mem results independent of the number of threads.
    • Check every alignment with flagstat, stats and mosdepth, and compare samples in MultiQC. Here about 99.8% of reads mapped, about 11% are duplicates, and mean depth is about 39x on chromosome 20.

    Content from 5A. Calling variants with bcftools

    Last updated on 2026-10-14 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 60 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How does bcftools turn aligned reads into genotype calls?
    • Why call the trio jointly?
    • How do we read a VCF record?

    Objectives

    • Explain what mpileup summarizes and how call turns it into genotypes and QUAL.
    • Call the trio jointly by region with an array job.
    • Concatenate, normalize (left-align, split multiallelic sites) and index the calls.
    • Read a VCF record (REF, ALT, QUAL, FILTER, INFO; GT, GQ, PL, AD, DP).

    Introduction

    In Episode 4 we looked at the reads at chr20:88,108 and guessed the genotype by eye. In this episode bcftools makes that guess for every position of chromosome 20, for all three samples at once, and writes the result as a VCF file. We start the calling job first, read a small example VCF while it runs, and then join, normalize and index our own calls.

    Prerequisite

    Before you start

    You need the three duplicate-marked BAM files and their indexes from Episode 4 in results/bam/, the reference links in ref/, and the script scripts/call.sh. If your alignment job did not finish, copy the BAM files from the results copy first (Episode 4, “Short on time?”).

    Live path (45 minutes; plan section 4: submit the calling array by about 11:40). Episodes 1-4 do not mark live and self-paced sections, so this note gives the live path; P7 applies the same format to every episode.

    Minutes Section Live or self-paced
    5 Step 1: submit call.sh; Step 3: start the interactive session live
    10 How bcftools calls a genotype (PL, prior, QUAL and GQ); joint calling live, short version
    15 Step 4: VCF anatomy on the example file; the chr20:88,108 record; challenge “Reading AD at a heterozygous site” live
    5 Step 5: a multiallelic site and normalization live
    10 Step 6: concatenate, normalize, count; challenge “SNVs and indels per sample” live

    Self-paced: Step 2 (the script line by line), the challenge “Predict a homozygous record”, and the callouts on the depth cap, ploidy and gVCF. If calling has not finished by the 35-minute mark, switch to the “Short on time?” copy and run Step 6 on it.

    Step 1: Submit the calling job

    The calling script is already in your scripts/ folder. Submit it now; the next sections explain it while it runs:

    BASH 

    cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/scripts
sbatch call.sh

    The script is an array job with eight tasks, one per region of chromosome 20, and each task uses 2 cores. In the workshop’s test runs each task took 2 to 4 minutes, plus the time waiting in the standby queue. Check on it with:

    BASH 

    squeue -u $USER

    Each task writes its log to scripts/cluster-call.<jobid>.out and .err.

    Callout

    Short on time?

    If your calling job fails or is still waiting when we reach Step 6, cancel it (scancel <jobid>) and copy the eight finished chunks and their indexes from the results copy:

    BASH 

    mkdir -p $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/vcf/chunks
cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/vcf/chunks/chunk0?.bcf* $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/vcf/chunks/

    Then continue with Step 6 as written.

    How bcftools calls a genotype

    Calling is two commands joined by a pipe (bcftools manual).

    bcftools mpileup reads the BAM files position by position. At each position it collects the bases of the reads that cover it, with their base qualities and mapping qualities, and computes for each sample a genotype likelihood for every possible genotype: how probable the observed bases are if the true genotype were 0/0, 0/1 or 1/1. It stores them in the PL field, Phred-scaled and rounded, so that the most likely genotype gets 0 and a genotype with PL 30 is 1,000 times less likely than that one (VCF specification, section 1.6.2). The statistical model is described by Li (2011).

    Before counting, mpileup drops some reads and bases. With the defaults of bcftools 1.24, as its usage text lists them:

    • reads with any of the flags UNMAP,SECONDARY,QCFAIL,DUP are skipped (--ns), so duplicates marked in Episode 4 do not count;
    • anomalous pairs, flagged as paired but not as a proper pair, are skipped (-A includes them);
    • reads with mapping quality below 0 are skipped (-q 0; that is, none are);
    • where the two reads of a pair overlap, the lower-quality base of each overlapping pair of bases gets base quality 0, so the overlap counts once (htslib sam.h, bam_mplp_init_overlaps; -x disables this);
    • bases with base quality below 1 are skipped (-Q 1), after the BAQ adjustment of Episode 3. Our data hold only the qualities 2, 11, 25 and 37 (Episode 3), so this floor removes only bases whose quality was set to 0, by BAQ or by the overlap rule;
    • at most 250 reads are read per position and input file (-d 250, the depth cap, see the callout below).

    bcftools call -m turns the likelihoods into calls. -m selects the “multiallelic caller”, which also handles sites with more than one ALT allele. It combines each sample’s likelihoods with a prior, the expected rate of variation (-P, default 1.1e-3, “mutation rate (use bigger for greater sensitivity)” in the usage text). From likelihoods and prior it decides whether the site is variant at all, and if so writes:

    • QUAL, for the site: the Phred-scaled probability that the site is not variant in any of the samples, “−10log10 prob(no variant)” in the VCF specification.
    • GT for each sample: the most probable genotype.
    • GQ for each sample, because call.sh asks for it with -a FORMAT/GQ: the Phred-scaled probability that this sample’s genotype is wrong, given that the site is variant (the specification’s “conditional genotype quality”).

    QUAL and GQ answer different questions. In a joint call of three samples, QUAL pools the evidence of all three: a site where only one sample carries the ALT allele can have a high QUAL, while another sample at the same site has a low GQ because few reads cover it. Filtering on QUAL judges the site; filtering on GQ judges one person’s genotype. Episode 6 uses both.

    -v writes variant sites only. Without it, every position of the chromosome would get a record.

    Callout

    Joint calling and per-sample calling

    We pass all three BAM files to one mpileup command, so the trio is called jointly: every site that is variant in any sample gets one record with a genotype for each of the three samples. Two things follow:

    • A sample without the ALT allele gets an explicit 0/0 with its own read counts, so “this person is homozygous for the reference allele, and we looked” is different from “no reads here” (./.). Episode 8 relies on this difference.
    • Evidence is pooled at the site level (QUAL), which helps at sites where one sample has few reads.

    Calling each sample separately and merging the VCFs afterwards loses the first point: a site missing from one sample’s VCF could be homozygous reference or simply not covered. The gVCF approach (callout at the end) solves this for large cohorts.

    Step 2: The calling script, line by line

    This is scripts/call.sh as you submitted it:

    BASH 

    #!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=2
#SBATCH --account=rcac
#SBATCH --qos=standby
#SBATCH --partition=cpu
#SBATCH --time=00:30:00
#SBATCH --job-name=call
#SBATCH --array=1-8
#SBATCH --output=cluster-%x.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=cluster-%x.%j.err

module load biocontainers
module load bcftools/1.24

WORK=$SCRATCH/varcall-workshop
REF=$WORK/ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa
BAMDIR=$WORK/results/bam
OUTDIR=$WORK/results/vcf/chunks
mkdir -p $OUTDIR

# One region of chr20 per array task (line N of the chunk list)
REGION=$(sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p" $WORK/resources/regions/chr20_chunks.txt)
CHUNK=chunk$(printf '%02d' $SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID)

# Joint calling of the trio; BAM order sets the sample order: child, father, mother
bcftools mpileup -f $REF -r $REGION -a AD,DP,SP -Ou \
    $BAMDIR/HG002.markdup.bam $BAMDIR/HG003.markdup.bam $BAMDIR/HG004.markdup.bam \
  | bcftools call -mv -a FORMAT/GQ -Ob -W -o $OUTDIR/$CHUNK.bcf

    Calling by region with an array job

    Calling works one position at a time and does not need the rest of the chromosome, so chromosome 20 can be split into regions that are called independently and joined afterwards. The region list has one region per line:

    BASH 

    cat $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/resources/regions/chr20_chunks.txt

    OUTPUT 

    chr20:1-8055521
chr20:8055522-16111042
chr20:16111043-24166563
chr20:24166564-31160372
chr20:31160373-40277604
chr20:40277605-48333125
chr20:48333126-56388646
chr20:56388647-64444167

    Eight regions in chrom:start-end form, 1-based and inclusive (Episode 2), in chromosome order. Together they cover chromosome 20 without overlap.

    Array task N reads line N of this list (sed -n "${SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID}p"; this file has no header, unlike samples.tsv), and names its output chunk01.bcf to chunk08.bcf (printf '%02d' pads the number to two digits). The regions were cut to hold similar amounts of sequence, so the tasks take similar times; the one that holds the centromere has the most calls and runs longest.

    The mpileup and call options

    Option Meaning
    -f $REF the reference FASTA. Its sequence names must match the BAM headers (chr20 in both)
    -r $REGION call only this region; needs the BAM indexes from Episode 4
    -a AD,DP,SP add per-sample allelic depths (AD), depth (DP) and a strand-bias score (SP)
    -Ou pass uncompressed BCF through the pipe
    three BAM files one sample each; their order is the order of the sample columns in the VCF
    call -m the multiallelic caller
    call -v write variant sites only
    -a FORMAT/GQ add the genotype quality
    -Ob -W -o write compressed BCF, write its index, and name the output file

    The sample names in the VCF come from the SM field of each BAM’s read group (Episode 4), and their order from the order of the BAM files: HG002 (child), HG003 (father), HG004 (mother), the order of trio.ped.

    Callout

    Why BCF for the chunks, and VCF for the result?

    BCF is the binary form of VCF: the same content, stored so that programs read it without parsing text. It is faster to write and read, which matters for intermediate files that only bcftools reads. The final file is bgzipped VCF (.vcf.gz), which other tools (hap.py, SnpEff, IGV) read and people can inspect with zcat or bcftools view. Both formats are compressed in blocks (BGZF), which lets an index (.csi or .tbi) jump straight to a region (htslib file formats). -W writes the index next to the output, so -r region queries work on every file we create.

    Step 3: Start an interactive session

    While the calling tasks run, start an interactive session and load bcftools. You will use the same session to join the chunks in Step 6:

    BASH 

    sinteractive -A rcac -q standby -p cpu -N 1 -n 4 --time=1:00:00
module load biocontainers
module load bcftools/1.24
cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop

    Step 4: Anatomy of a VCF record

    Your own calls are not ready yet, so we read a small example first: resources/example/trio.example.raw.vcf.gz holds the calls of the workshop’s reference run for chr20:60,000-90,000, before normalization. It contains the three sites of Episodes 2 and 4.

    A VCF file has a header (lines starting with ##, then one line starting with #CHROM) and one line per variant. The header declares every field the records use. Print the declarations of the fields we need, and the column line:

    BASH 

    bcftools view -h resources/example/trio.example.raw.vcf.gz | grep -E '^##(INFO|FORMAT)=<ID=(DP|MQ|AD|GT|PL|GQ),'
bcftools view -h resources/example/trio.example.raw.vcf.gz | tail -1

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
##INFO=<ID=DP,Number=1,Type=Integer,Description="Raw read depth">
##FORMAT=<ID=PL,Number=G,Type=Integer,Description="List of Phred-scaled genotype likelihoods">
##FORMAT=<ID=DP,Number=1,Type=Integer,Description="Number of high-quality bases">
##FORMAT=<ID=AD,Number=R,Type=Integer,Description="Allelic depths (high-quality bases)">
##FORMAT=<ID=GT,Number=1,Type=String,Description="Genotype">
##FORMAT=<ID=GQ,Number=1,Type=Integer,Description="Phred-scaled Genotype Quality">
##INFO=<ID=MQ,Number=1,Type=Integer,Description="Average mapping quality">
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
#CHROM	POS	ID	REF	ALT	QUAL	FILTER	INFO	FORMAT	HG002	HG003	HG004

    The [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] lines are a warning that bcftools prints for these files; the callout in Step 6 explains it. Each ##INFO and ##FORMAT line gives a field’s ID, how many values it has (Number: 1, R for one per allele including REF, G for one per possible genotype), its type and a description. INFO fields describe the site; FORMAT fields are repeated for each sample. The last line names the columns: eight fixed columns, FORMAT, then one column per sample.

    Now the record at the heterozygous site of Episode 4:

    BASH 

    bcftools view -H -r chr20:88108 resources/example/trio.example.raw.vcf.gz

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
chr20	88108	.	T	C	723.977	.	DP=117;VDB=0.244275;SGB=-7.53767;RPBZ=-1.26517;MQBZ=0;MQSBZ=0;BQBZ=0.232513;SCBZ=0;MQ0F=0;AC=3;AN=6;DP4=30,23,31,23;MQ=60	GT:PL:DP:SP:AD:GQ	0/1:249,0,255:32:8:19,13:127	0/1:255,0,255:42:4:20,22:127	0/1:255,0,255:33:16:14,19:127

    Reading it column by column (VCF specification, section 1.6):

    Column Here Meaning
    CHROM, POS chr20, 88108 1-based position
    ID . no identifier (for example a dbSNP rs number)
    REF, ALT T, C reference allele and the alternate allele(s)
    QUAL about 724 site quality (above)
    FILTER . not filtered yet; Episode 6 fills this column
    INFO DP=...;...;MQ=... site-level fields, separated by ;
    FORMAT GT:PL:DP:SP:AD:GQ the order of the per-sample fields that follow
    HG002, HG003, HG004 0/1:... one column per sample, values in the FORMAT order

    So the HG002 column reads as: GT the genotype; PL the three genotype likelihoods for 0/0, 0/1, 1/1; DP this sample’s depth; SP the strand-bias score; AD the read counts for REF and ALT; GQ the genotype quality. PL and GQ stop at 255 and 127 in these files: a value at the cap means “at least this confident”.

    Challenge

    Challenge: reading AD at a heterozygous site

    1. From the record above, what are HG002’s AD and DP at chr20:88,108? How many reads support C?
    2. In Episode 4, samtools tview showed 14 reads with C and 25 with the reference T in this column, 39 in all. Do the numbers agree? If not, list what mpileup does that tview does not.
    3. The INFO field also has a DP. Why is it larger than HG002’s DP?

    1. HG002 has AD 19,13 and DP 32: 13 reads support C.

    2. They differ, because mpileup counts only some of the reads that tview displays. The workshop’s test run counted the same position with each of mpileup’s read and base filters switched off, then on again one at a time:

      What mpileup counts at chr20:88,108 in HG002 AD (T,C) and DP
      every read and base, filters off 25,14,0; DP 39
      skip reads flagged as duplicates 21,14,0; DP 35
      also skip anomalous pairs (paired, not in a proper pair) 21,14,0; DP 35
      also detect overlapping mates (one base of each overlap gets quality 0) 21,14,0; DP 35
      also apply the base-quality floor (-Q 1) 19,13,0; DP 32
      also apply BAQ: the defaults, as in call.sh 19,13,0; DP 32

      Each row adds one filter to the row above (the third number of AD counts bases that are neither T nor C). The options are those of the bcftools 1.24 usage text (--ns, -A, -x, -Q, -B). With every filter off, mpileup counts the same 39 reads as the tview column, 25 T and 14 C. Two causes explain the difference at this site:

      • duplicates: 4 reads, all T, are marked as duplicates (Episode 4) and skipped;
      • overlapping mates: in 3 read pairs both mates cover the site. Overlap detection sets one base of each pair to quality 0, which changes no count by itself (the overlap row), and the base-quality floor then drops those 3 bases (2 T, 1 C).

      Anomalous pairs and BAQ remove nothing here. That leaves 19 T and 13 C, 32 in all.

    3. INFO/DP (117) is the site’s raw depth summed over all three samples; FORMAT/DP is one sample’s depth after the filters above. The header lines from the start of this step give both descriptions. Episode 6 filters on each, so it matters which one an expression reads.

    Why 0/1: the likelihood argument

    In Episode 4 we reasoned with a coin toss: with 39 reads at a balanced heterozygous site, 14 or fewer C reads happen 5.4% of the time (10.8% for 14 or fewer of either allele). That is a tail probability, and it does not by itself decide anything. The caller compares the three genotypes instead. HG002’s PL at this site is 249,0,255:

    • 0/0 would mean that all 13 C bases are sequencing errors, each of them at high base quality. That is extremely unlikely, so its PL is large.
    • 1/1 would mean that all the T bases are errors. Also extremely unlikely.
    • 0/1 explains both alleles with ordinary sampling, so its PL is 0.

    A difference of 10 in PL is a factor of 10 in likelihood, so a difference in the hundreds means that the other genotypes are less likely by many orders of magnitude. The call is 0/1 because the alternatives are far less likely, not because 14 of 39 passes a test of balance. GQ (at the cap, 127) says the same.

    Challenge

    Challenge: predict a homozygous record

    The benchmark says HG002 is homozygous for the ALT allele A at chr20:85,259 (reference G), and in Episode 4 all 50 reads in that column showed A.

    1. Before you look: what do you expect for HG002’s GT, the two numbers of AD, and which of the three PL values is 0?
    2. Check with bcftools query, which prints the fields you name in the format you give it (% for a field, [...] repeated for each sample):

    BASH 

    bcftools query -r chr20:85259 -f '%POS %REF %ALT %QUAL[\n  %SAMPLE %GT AD=%AD DP=%DP PL=%PL GQ=%GQ]\n' resources/example/trio.example.raw.vcf.gz

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
85259 G A 739.009
  HG002 1/1 AD=0,43 DP=43 PL=255,129,0 GQ=127
  HG003 1/1 AD=0,38 DP=38 PL=255,114,0 GQ=127
  HG004 1/1 AD=0,32 DP=32 PL=255,96,0 GQ=127

    HG002 is 1/1 with AD 0,43, DP 43, PL 255,129,0 and GQ 127. No read supports G, and the third PL value (for 1/1) is 0. If your prediction had AD equal to 0,50: mpileup counts fewer reads than tview shows, for the reasons in the previous challenge.

    bcftools query turns a VCF into a table, which is how most questions about a call set are answered. One table with the genotypes of all three samples at the three sites from Episode 4 (the het SNV, the hom-ALT SNV and a 10 bp insertion):

    BASH 

    bcftools query -r chr20:85259,chr20:86859,chr20:88108 -f '%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%QUAL[\t%SAMPLE=%GT]\n' resources/example/trio.example.raw.vcf.gz

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
85259	G	A	739.009	HG002=1/1	HG003=1/1	HG004=1/1
86859	TTGGTAT	TTGGTATCTAGTGGTAT	729.329	HG002=1/1	HG003=1/1	HG004=0/1
88108	T	C	723.977	HG002=0/1	HG003=0/1	HG004=0/1

    Step 5: Variant representation and normalization

    The same variant can be written in more than one way. A deletion inside a repeat can be placed at any copy of the repeat unit, and a site with two different ALT alleles can be one record (ALT = A,T) or two. Tools that compare calls by position and allele, such as bcftools isec (bcftools manual), see different representations as different variants. Normalization gives each variant one form (Tan et al. 2015):

    • left-alignment: shift each indel to its leftmost equivalent position and trim shared bases; this needs the reference (norm -f);
    • splitting: write each ALT allele of a multiallelic site as its own record (norm -m -any).

    The example region has one multiallelic site before normalization. Find it:

    BASH 

    bcftools query -i 'N_ALT>1' -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%QUAL[\t%SAMPLE=%GT:%AD]\n' resources/example/trio.example.raw.vcf.gz

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
chr20	88865	GACACACACACACACACACACACACACACA	GACACACACACACACACACACACACACACACACACA,GACACACACACACACACACACACACACACACACA	240.617	HG002=0/0:36,0,0	HG003=0/2:26,0,4	HG004=0/1:15,17,0

    -i 'N_ALT>1' keeps records with more than one ALT allele. This one is in a CA repeat: the two ALT alleles add 6 and 4 bases to it (ACACAC and ACAC). Genotypes number the alleles in order, 0 for REF, 1 for the first ALT and 2 for the second, and AD has one number per allele in the same order. So HG003 is 0/2 (26 reads for REF, 4 for the second ALT), HG004 is 0/1 (15 and 17), and the child HG002 is 0/0. Now look at the same position in the normalized version of the example, trio.example.filtered.vcf.gz (it is also filtered, which Episode 6 explains). The first line stores the position in a shell variable:

    BASH 

    POS=$(bcftools query -i 'N_ALT>1' -f '%POS\n' resources/example/trio.example.raw.vcf.gz)
bcftools query -r chr20:$POS -f '%CHROM\t%POS\t%REF\t%ALT\t%QUAL[\t%SAMPLE=%GT:%AD]\n' resources/example/trio.example.filtered.vcf.gz

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
chr20	88865	G	GACACAC	240.617	HG002=0/0:36,0	HG003=0/0:26,0	HG004=0/1:15,17
chr20	88865	G	GACAC	240.617	HG002=0/0:36,0	HG003=0/1:26,4	HG004=0/0:15,0

    The one record became 2 records at the same position, each with a single ALT allele, and norm also trimmed the repeat bases that REF and ALT shared, so each insertion is now written as G followed by the inserted bases. A sample’s genotype is rewritten for each record: HG003’s 0/2 becomes 0/0 in the first record and 0/1 in the second, because when splitting, norm fills in the reference allele for the other ALT (--multi-overlaps 0|., default [0], in the 1.24 usage text). In the same way a 1/2 would become 1/0 and 0/1. AD keeps the REF count and the count of that record’s ALT: HG003’s 4 reads for the shorter insertion appear only in the second record. Reads of the other ALT count as neither allele, so read the AD of split records with care.

    After splitting, every record is biallelic, which makes counting simple (one ALT, one variant), and Episodes 6-8 can treat each record as one variant.

    Step 6: Join, normalize and index the calls

    When squeue -u $USER no longer lists the call job, continue in your session. First, list the chunks in order:

    BASH 

    # chunk01 ... chunk08: the names sort in chromosome order
ls results/vcf/chunks/chunk*.bcf > results/vcf/chunks.txt
cat results/vcf/chunks.txt

    OUTPUT 

    results/vcf/chunks/chunk01.bcf
results/vcf/chunks/chunk02.bcf
results/vcf/chunks/chunk03.bcf
results/vcf/chunks/chunk04.bcf
results/vcf/chunks/chunk05.bcf
results/vcf/chunks/chunk06.bcf
results/vcf/chunks/chunk07.bcf
results/vcf/chunks/chunk08.bcf

    Because the chunk numbers are padded to two digits, ls lists them in chromosome order. Join them, then normalize:

    BASH 

    bcftools concat -f results/vcf/chunks.txt -Ob -W -o results/vcf/trio.raw.bcf
bcftools norm -f ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa -m -any -Oz -W -o results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz results/vcf/trio.raw.bcf

    OUTPUT 

    Checking the headers and starting positions of 8 files
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
Concatenating results/vcf/chunks/chunk01.bcf	0.105096 seconds
Concatenating results/vcf/chunks/chunk02.bcf	0.088082 seconds
Concatenating results/vcf/chunks/chunk03.bcf	0.084996 seconds
Concatenating results/vcf/chunks/chunk04.bcf	0.271559 seconds
Concatenating results/vcf/chunks/chunk05.bcf	0.092314 seconds
Concatenating results/vcf/chunks/chunk06.bcf	0.079879 seconds
Concatenating results/vcf/chunks/chunk07.bcf	0.095996 seconds
Concatenating results/vcf/chunks/chunk08.bcf	0.106483 seconds
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
Lines   total/split/joined/realigned/mismatch_removed/dup_removed/skipped:	181481/3956/0/28035/0/0/0

    concat first checks the headers and the starting position of each file; the files must be listed in chromosome order. norm reports what it did on its Lines line: the number of records read, how many multiallelic records it split (3,956), and how many indels it realigned (28,035). The seconds on the Concatenating lines differ from run to run.

    concat -f reads the list of files to join, in order. norm -f left-aligns indels against the reference, and -m -any splits every multiallelic site, SNVs and indels alike. Both write with -W, so both outputs get an index.

    Callout

    “MQ should be declared as Type=Float”

    Every bcftools command that reads these files prints:

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float

    It is a header-type notice, not an error. The VCF specification reserves the INFO key MQ (“RMS mapping quality”) with Type=Float (VCF specification, Table 1), and the header that mpileup writes declares MQ with another type (the ##INFO=<ID=MQ line in Step 4). The warning changes nothing in the output: the INFO/MQ < 30 filter in Episode 6 flags 6,407 sites, as expected from the MQ distribution. You can ignore it.

    Check the sample names and the first records:

    bcftools query -l results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz
bcftools view -H results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz | head -3

    Your record at chr20:88,108 should be identical to the one in the example file, because the example was cut from the reference run, made with the same scripts:

    bcftools view -H -r chr20:88108 results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
chr20	88108	.	T	C	723.977	.	DP=117;VDB=0.244275;SGB=-7.53767;RPBZ=-1.26517;MQBZ=0;MQSBZ=0;BQBZ=0.232513;SCBZ=0;MQ0F=0;AC=3;AN=6;DP4=30,23,31,23;MQ=60	GT:PL:DP:SP:AD:GQ	0/1:249,0,255:32:8:19,13:127	0/1:255,0,255:42:4:20,22:127	0/1:255,0,255:33:16:14,19:127

    Count the calls

    bcftools stats summarizes a VCF file. -s - adds per-sample counts for all samples. Save the summary, then print the overall numbers and the per-sample lines:

    BASH 

    bcftools stats -s - results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz > results/vcf/trio.norm.stats.txt
grep -E '^(SN|TSTV)' results/vcf/trio.norm.stats.txt
grep ^PSC results/vcf/trio.norm.stats.txt

    OUTPUT

    The SN lines count records by type: 185,914 records, 155,291 SNVs and 30,623 indels, and no multiallelic sites left after norm. The TSTV line gives the transition/transversion ratio of the SNVs, 1.81 (Episode 6 explains why it matters). Each PSC line describes one sample; its columns are listed in the comment line above them in the stats file (grep -m1 '^# PSC' results/vcf/trio.norm.stats.txt).

    Challenge

    Challenge: SNVs and indels per sample

    The trio file has 155,291 SNV records and 30,623 indel records, but no single person carries all of them.

    1. From the PSC lines, how many SNVs and how many indels does each sample carry? (SNVs are transitions plus transversions; use the # PSC comment line to find the columns.)
    2. Why does each sample carry fewer than the trio file holds?
    3. Which column counts the genotypes with no call (./.)?
    1. HG002 119,856 SNVs and 21,759 indels; HG003 117,758 SNVs and 21,267 indels; HG004 118,664 SNVs and 21,684 indels. For HG002, 76,976 transitions plus 42,880 transversions give 119,856.
    2. A trio record is written when any of the three samples carries an ALT allele; at many sites only one or two of them do. A sample with 0/0 or ./. at a site does not carry that variant.
    3. nMissing, the last column: HG002 298, HG003 262 and HG004 449 missing genotypes. Before filtering, a genotype is missing only where the sample has no usable reads.

    Type exit to leave the interactive session.

    Callout

    Short on time?

    If you could not join and normalize the calls, copy the result and its statistics from the results copy:

    BASH 

    cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz* $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/vcf/
cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/vcf/trio.norm.stats.txt $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/vcf/

    Episode 6 starts from results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz.

    Callout

    The depth cap

    mpileup reads at most 250 reads per position from each input file (-d). At about 40x this never matters in ordinary sequence. It matters in two cases. In a collapsed repeat, many copies of a sequence that the reference holds only once, reads from all copies pile up at one place. Depth far above the mean does occur in our data: in Episode 4, mosdepth reported a maximum depth of 13,784 in HG002. At such places the cap keeps memory in check, and the calls deserve suspicion anyway; Episode 6 flags sites with unusually high depth. In deep data (targeted panels, amplicons, mitochondria), the cap silently throws away reads at every position; raise -d for such data.

    Callout

    Ploidy

    Human chromosome 20 is diploid, so every genotype here has two alleles. bcftools call assumes diploid genotypes unless told otherwise; its usage text gives --ploidy the default [2]. For haploid sequence (chrY and most of chrX in males, mitochondria, many microbes) or polyploid organisms, set --ploidy or --ploidy-file. Pooled samples need a different approach altogether (Episode 10).

    Callout

    The gVCF idea

    Our VCF has records only at variant sites (-v). To add a fourth sample later, we would have to call all four again, because the existing file does not say whether the new sample’s variant sites were covered in the other three. A gVCF solves this: it also stores blocks of non-variant positions with their depth and genotype quality, so each sample is called once and the samples are genotyped together afterwards. bcftools mpileup -g writes gVCF blocks, and GATK’s HaplotypeCaller is built around them; Episode 5B (self-paced) uses that route.

    Common problems

    Symptom Likely cause Fix
    errors that name a sequence, or an empty VCF contig names differ between FASTA and BAM (chr20 against 20), or a different reference build align to the same FASTA you call with; check samtools view -H against the .fai (Episode 2)
    no AD in the FORMAT column -a AD missing from mpileup add -a AD,DP,SP as in call.sh
    millions of records, nearly all 0/0 -v missing from call call again with -mv
    mpileup reports a region it cannot parse region syntax: chr20:1-8060000, no spaces, no thousands separators fix the line in the region list
    depth stuck at 250 in deep data the depth cap raise -d
    concat complains about the order of the files chunks listed out of order list them in chromosome order (the padded names do this)
    “could not load index” or -r does not work an output written without an index write with -W, or run bcftools index
    one sample column, or unexpected sample names wrong SM in the read groups fix samples.tsv and realign (Episode 4)

    Summary

    Key Points
    • bcftools mpileup computes per-sample genotype likelihoods (PL) from the bases, base qualities and mapping qualities of the reads; it skips duplicates and some other reads and bases by default.
    • bcftools call -m combines the likelihoods with a prior to give GT for each sample and QUAL for the site; GQ is added on request (-a FORMAT/GQ).
    • QUAL is about the site, pooled over the samples of a joint call; GQ is about one sample’s genotype.
    • Joint calling gives every sample a genotype at every variant site, so homozygous reference is distinct from no data.
    • Calling by region with an array job, then concat in order, norm -f -m -any and indexing (-W), gives one normalized, indexed VCF.
    • A genotype is chosen because the alternatives are much less likely (PL), not because the read counts pass a balance test.

    Content from 6. Filtering and evaluating variant calls

    Last updated on 2026-10-14 | Edit this page

    Estimated time: 80 minutes

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do we summarize a call set?
    • How do we choose and apply filters?
    • How good are our calls, and how do we know?
    • What can we measure when there is no truth set?

    Objectives

    • Summarize a call set (counts, Ts/Tv, het/hom-alt ratio, indel lengths, depth and QUAL distributions).
    • Apply soft filters at the site and genotype levels.
    • Measure precision and recall against a GIAB benchmark in its confident regions.
    • Explain the precision-recall trade-off of a threshold and why indels and difficult regions do worse.
    • Choose proxy measures when no truth set exists.

    Introduction

    The caller reports every site where the evidence favors a variant, including many that are wrong. In this episode we decide which calls to trust. We look at the distributions of the quality measures, choose thresholds from them, and label the calls that fail. Then we measure how good the calls are, before and after filtering, against the Genome in a Bottle benchmark for HG002, and look at what we can measure when no benchmark exists.

    The order matters: thresholds come from the call set, and the benchmark only evaluates them. Choosing a threshold because it scores best against the benchmark would tune the filters to the answer key, and the score would no longer tell us how well they work on other data.

    Prerequisite

    Before you start

    You need results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz and its index from Episode 5A, and the script scripts/evaluate.sh. If you do not have them, use the “Short on time?” copy at the end of Episode 5A.

    Live path (60 minutes; plan section 4, with hap.py running in the background):

    Minutes Section Live or self-paced
    5 Step 1: session and distributions live
    10 Step 2: thresholds from the distributions; the filter commands live
    7 Step 3: site and genotype filters, and what they changed live
    3 Step 4: submit task 1 of evaluate.sh; copy the other three tasks’ results live
    10 While hap.py runs: Ts/Tv inside and outside the benchmark (end of Step 3); benchmarks, precision and recall live
    10 Step 5: reading summary.csv; the genotype mask and the site filters live
    7 Challenge “Predict, then test a QUAL threshold” and the leakage callout live
    8 Discussion “Same calls, two benchmarks”; proxies without a truth set live, discussion

    Self-paced: the challenge “Predict the filters”, the Ts/Tv challenge with PASS calls, the challenge “Same calls, two benchmarks” (the live session uses it as a discussion), and the sections on stratification and on proxies beyond Ts/Tv.

    Step 1: Look at the distributions

    Start an interactive session and write two tables: the site-level QUAL, depth (INFO/DP) and mean mapping quality (INFO/MQ) of every record, and the depth and GQ of every genotype:

    BASH 

    sinteractive -A rcac -q standby -p cpu -N 1 -n 4 --time=1:00:00
module load biocontainers
module load bcftools/1.24
cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop
VCF=results/vcf/trio.norm.vcf.gz
mkdir -p results/vcf/stats
bcftools query -f '%QUAL\t%INFO/DP\t%INFO/MQ\n' $VCF > results/vcf/stats/site_qual_dp_mq.tsv
bcftools query -f '[%SAMPLE\t%GT\t%DP\t%GQ\n]' $VCF > results/vcf/stats/genotype_dp_gq.tsv

    The [...] in the second format repeats for each sample, so that table has one line per sample per record. Summarize the site table with a few percentiles: sort one column, then print the values 1%, 5%, 50%, 95% and 99% of the way through:

    BASH 

    cut -f1 results/vcf/stats/site_qual_dp_mq.tsv | sort -g | awk '{ v[NR] = $1 } END { print "QUAL", "p01", v[int(NR * 0.01)], "p05", v[int(NR * 0.05)], "p50", v[int(NR * 0.5)], "p95", v[int(NR * 0.95)], "p99", v[int(NR * 0.99)] }'
cut -f2 results/vcf/stats/site_qual_dp_mq.tsv | sort -g | awk '{ v[NR] = $1 } END { print "DP", "p01", v[int(NR * 0.01)], "p05", v[int(NR * 0.05)], "p50", v[int(NR * 0.5)], "p95", v[int(NR * 0.95)], "p99", v[int(NR * 0.99)] }'
cut -f3 results/vcf/stats/site_qual_dp_mq.tsv | sort -g | awk '{ v[NR] = $1 } END { print "MQ", "p01", v[int(NR * 0.01)], "p05", v[int(NR * 0.05)], "p50", v[int(NR * 0.5)], "p95", v[int(NR * 0.95)], "p99", v[int(NR * 0.99)] }'

    OUTPUT 

    QUAL p01 6.9928 p05 38.8882 p50 469.376 p95 739.009 p99 741.877
DP p01 19 p05 69 p50 113 p95 358 p99 668
MQ p01 11 p05 35 p50 60 p95 60 p99 60

    Read each line as a shape:

    • QUAL has a long low tail: most sites are far above 30, but the lowest few percent are not (p05 is 38.9 and p01 7.0).
    • Depth has a long high tail: the median site depth (all three samples together) is close to three times the 39x of each sample, but p95 and p99 are several times the median (median 113, p95 358, p99 668). Sites with far more reads than the genome has copies are typical of reads from several places piled onto one, as in collapsed repeats (Episode 5A).
    • MQ, the mean mapping quality of the reads at a site, sits at 60 for most sites and has a low tail where reads may come from elsewhere in the genome (Episode 4).

    Step 2: Choose thresholds from the data

    Each filter targets one of those tails, with a threshold set by a rule or a convention, not by the benchmark:

    Filter Rule Why this value
    LowQual: QUAL < 30 a convention QUAL is Phred-scaled (Episode 5A): 30 means a 1 in 1,000 chance that the site is not variant at all. It cuts the low tail
    HighDP: INFO/DP above twice the median site depth a rule, computed from your own calls at twice the expected depth, more reads arrive than two copies of the sequence explain. The value adapts to any depth, so the rule carries over to other data
    LowMQ: INFO/MQ < 30 a convention MAPQ is Phred-scaled (SAM specification): MAPQ 30 means a 1 in 1,000 chance that a read is misplaced. A site whose reads average below 30 has many reads placed with little confidence
    genotype mask: FMT/DP < 10 or FMT/GQ < 20 conventions with fewer than 10 reads, a heterozygous site looks homozygous about 0.2% of the time (2 x 0.5^10 = 0.195%, Episode 1); GQ 20 is a 1% chance that the genotype is wrong

    The depth threshold is computed in the next block: sort the site depths, take the middle value, double it.

    BASH 

    # The depth cutoff follows a rule, not the benchmark: flag sites deeper than twice the median
MEDIAN_DP=$(cut -f2 results/vcf/stats/site_qual_dp_mq.tsv | sort -n | awk '{ d[NR] = $1 } END { print d[int((NR + 1) / 2)] }')
MAX_DP=$((2 * MEDIAN_DP))
echo "median site depth $MEDIAN_DP; sites above $MAX_DP are flagged HighDP"

    OUTPUT 

    median site depth 113; sites above 226 are flagged HighDP

    In the reference run the median site depth was 113, so MAX_DP was 226. Yours is computed from your own calls, so if your calls differ, so does the threshold.

    Challenge

    Challenge: predict the filters

    Before applying the filters, count how many sites each site filter will flag, and how many genotypes the mask will set to missing in each sample:

    BASH 

    awk '$1 < 30' results/vcf/stats/site_qual_dp_mq.tsv | wc -l
awk -v max=$MAX_DP '$2 > max' results/vcf/stats/site_qual_dp_mq.tsv | wc -l
awk '$3 < 30' results/vcf/stats/site_qual_dp_mq.tsv | wc -l
awk '$3 < 10 || $4 < 20' results/vcf/stats/genotype_dp_gq.tsv | cut -f1 | sort | uniq -c
    1. Which site filter flags the most sites?
    2. Will the three site filters together flag the sum of the three counts? Why or why not?
    3. The last command counts genotypes with low depth or low GQ. Will the mask set exactly these genotypes to missing?

    OUTPUT 

    7622
17821
6407
  11564 HG002
  10934 HG003
  11167 HG004
    1. HighDP: 17,821 sites, against 7,622 with QUAL below 30 and 6,407 with MQ below 30.
    2. No. A site can fail more than one filter, and it is counted once in each list. Step 3 shows the combinations.
    3. Yes. Compare with the nMissing counts in Step 3: they are the same numbers (HG002 11,564, HG003 10,934, HG004 11,167). The count includes the genotypes that were already missing before filtering (Episode 5A; 298 in HG002), which have low depth too; the mask sets the others to missing. In the workshop’s test run, most of HG002’s newly masked genotypes failed on GQ alone (7,639 of 11,266), 1,920 on depth alone and 1,707 on both.

    Step 3: Site-level and genotype-level filters

    Apply the filters. The first three commands label sites; the last one masks genotypes:

    BASH 

    # 2. Site filters add a label to FILTER and keep the record; the genotype filter sets
#    genotypes with DP < 10 or GQ < 20 to missing (./.)
bcftools filter -m+ -s LowQual -e 'QUAL<30' -Ou $VCF \
  | bcftools filter -m+ -s HighDP -e "INFO/DP>$MAX_DP" -Ou \
  | bcftools filter -m+ -s LowMQ -e 'INFO/MQ<30' -Ou \
  | bcftools filter -S . -e 'FMT/DP<10 | FMT/GQ<20' -Oz -W -o results/vcf/trio.filtered.vcf.gz

    What each part does (bcftools manual, filter, and the 1.24 usage text):

    • -e EXPR names what fails: records for which the expression is true. (-i is the opposite: it names what passes. Swapping them inverts a filter.)
    • -s NAME makes a soft filter: a failing record gets NAME in its FILTER column and stays in the file. A record that passes gets PASS. Without -s (and without -S), failing records would be deleted: a hard filter, which you cannot undo or inspect later.
    • -m+ adds the new label to labels already there (“do not replace but add to existing FILTER”), so a site that fails two filters reads LowQual;HighDP.
    • The first three filters read site-level values: QUAL, and INFO/DP and INFO/MQ, which describe all reads at the site, from all three samples.
    • The last command reads genotype-level values: FMT/DP and FMT/GQ, one per sample. With -S . it sets the genotypes of the failing samples to missing (./.), and it has no -s, so it adds no FILTER label and removes no record.

    How does an expression on FORMAT fields combine across three samples? The bcftools manual says that with a single & or |, both conditions are tested within one sample, and the expression selects the samples for which it is true; && and || let the conditions be met in different samples. So FMT/DP<10 | FMT/GQ<20 selects each sample whose own depth is below 10 or whose own GQ is below 20, and -S . masks exactly those samples’ genotypes. The other samples at the same site keep their calls.

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float

    bcftools view -H results/vcf/trio.filtered.vcf.gz | cut -f7 | sort | uniq -c

    Finally, summarize the records that PASS, as Episode 5A did for all records:

    BASH 

    bcftools stats -f PASS -s - results/vcf/trio.filtered.vcf.gz > results/vcf/trio.filtered.stats.txt
grep -E '^(SN|TSTV)' results/vcf/trio.filtered.stats.txt

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
SN	0	number of samples:	3
SN	0	number of records:	158151
SN	0	number of no-ALTs:	0
SN	0	number of SNPs:	129329
SN	0	number of MNPs:	0
SN	0	number of indels:	28822
SN	0	number of others:	0
SN	0	number of multiallelic sites:	0

TSTV	0	86429	42900	2.01	86429	42900	2.01

    158,151 PASS records, 129,329 SNVs and 28,822 indels. Ts/Tv rises from 1.81 for all records to 2.01 for the PASS records.

    What Ts/Tv tells us

    A transition exchanges a purine for a purine or a pyrimidine for a pyrimidine (A and G, C and T); a transversion is any other change. Of the three possible changes at a base, one is a transition and two are transversions, so random errors give a Ts/Tv near 0.5. Real human germline variation has more transitions than transversions: in the HG002 benchmark’s own SNVs on chromosome 20, Ts/Tv is 2.31 inside the v4.2.1 regions (reference run, TRUTH.TOTAL.TiTv_ratio). A call set with many errors has a Ts/Tv pulled toward 0.5. That is why filtering raised it from 1.81 to 2.01: the filters removed relatively more transversions, the signature of errors. Ts/Tv works only as a comparison (before and after, inside and outside, one sample against another); it does not say how many calls are wrong.

    Ts/Tv inside and outside the benchmark regions

    The last two commands of the session compute Ts/Tv for HG002’s calls (raw, before filtering) inside the regions where the v4.2.1 benchmark is confident (-T with the BED file), and outside them (^ negates the regions):

    BASH 

    # 3. Ts/Tv of HG002's raw calls inside and outside the benchmark regions (^ means outside)
bcftools view -s HG002 -c 1 -Ou $VCF | bcftools stats -T resources/truth/HG002_v4.2.1_chr20.bed - | grep ^TSTV
bcftools view -s HG002 -c 1 -Ou $VCF | bcftools stats -T ^resources/truth/HG002_v4.2.1_chr20.bed - | grep ^TSTV

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
TSTV	0	50100	21960	2.28	50100	21960	2.28
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
TSTV	0	26876	20920	1.28	26876	20920	1.28

    Each line gives the numbers of transitions and transversions, then their ratio. Inside the benchmark regions it is close to the truth set’s 2.31; outside, it is far lower (2.28 inside, 1.28 outside).

    view -s HG002 -c 1 keeps HG002’s column and only the records where HG002 carries at least one ALT allele (Step 4 explains why). The benchmark regions are where NIST is confident it knows the truth; outside them lies sequence that NIST could not yet characterize, which includes difficult repeats (“Same calls, two benchmarks” below returns to this). A low Ts/Tv outside means many of the calls there are errors, and that is where a benchmark cannot score them.

    Challenge

    Challenge: do the filters help where the benchmark cannot look?

    Repeat the two commands for HG002’s PASS calls. -f PASS keeps only records that pass every filter, and -Ou passes the result through the pipe:

    BASH 

    bcftools view -s HG002 -c 1 -f PASS -Ou results/vcf/trio.filtered.vcf.gz | bcftools stats -T resources/truth/HG002_v4.2.1_chr20.bed - | grep ^TSTV
bcftools view -s HG002 -c 1 -f PASS -Ou results/vcf/trio.filtered.vcf.gz | bcftools stats -T ^resources/truth/HG002_v4.2.1_chr20.bed - | grep ^TSTV
    1. How does Ts/Tv change inside and outside the benchmark regions after filtering?
    2. Why does it change more outside?
    3. The staged file resources/regions/chr20_centromere.bed holds the centromere of chromosome 20. Write the command for HG002’s raw calls in the centromere, and predict the result.

    OUTPUT 

    [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
TSTV	0	49743	21630	2.30	49743	21630	2.30
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
TSTV	0	15059	10458	1.44	15059	10458	1.44

    1. Inside, it barely moves (2.28 to 2.30); outside, it rises (1.28 to 1.44).

    2. Inside the benchmark regions few calls are wrong, so there is little to remove. Outside, many calls are errors, and the filters remove relatively more of them. The benchmark could never show this, because it does not score calls outside its regions.

    3. Replace the BED file:

      BASH 

      bcftools view -s HG002 -c 1 -Ou $VCF | bcftools stats -T resources/regions/chr20_centromere.bed - | grep ^TSTV

      OUTPUT 

      [W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
[W::bcf_hdr_check_sanity] MQ should be declared as Type=Float
TSTV	0	14759	12135	1.22	14759	12135	1.22

      HG002 has 26,894 raw SNVs in the centromere (14,759 transitions plus 12,135 transversions), 22% of its 119,856 SNVs in 5.6% of the chromosome, with Ts/Tv 1.22. In the reference run, 12,390 of them PASS after filtering, with Ts/Tv 1.36: still far from 2.3. The filters remove many calls there and improve the ratio, but many remaining calls in the centromere are likely errors.

    Type exit to leave the interactive session.

    Callout

    Short on time?

    If filtering did not finish, copy the filtered calls and the tables from the results copy:

    BASH 

    cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/vcf/trio.filtered.vcf.gz* $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/vcf/
cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/vcf/trio.filtered.stats.txt $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/vcf/

    Benchmarking against Genome in a Bottle

    To measure accuracy we need the right answer. For HG002, NIST publishes benchmark variant calls and the confident regions (a BED file) where it vouches for them (Genome in a Bottle). Inside those regions, every variant in the benchmark is real, and every position not in it is homozygous reference. Outside them, the benchmark says nothing.

    Comparing our calls with the benchmark sorts them into:

    • true positives (TP): in both;
    • false positives (FP): in our calls, not in the benchmark;
    • false negatives (FN): in the benchmark, missed by our calls.

    From these (Krusche et al. 2019):

    • precision = TP / (TP + FP): the fraction of our calls that are right;
    • recall = TP / (TP + FN): the fraction of real variants we found;
    • F1 = 2 x precision x recall / (precision + recall): one number that is high only if both are.

    A variant called with the wrong genotype (for example 0/1 where the benchmark says 1/1) counts as both a false positive and a false negative.

    Comparing variants is harder than comparing positions

    The same variant can be written in several ways (Episode 5A), especially indels in repeats and nearby variants that can be grouped differently. hap.py with the vcfeval engine compares the haplotypes, the sequences the variants produce, rather than the text of the records, so equivalent representations match (hap.py documentation). Normalization still matters for everything that compares records by position and allele: counting variants, merging files, and tools such as bcftools isec.

    Step 4: Evaluate with hap.py

    This is scripts/evaluate.sh:

    BASH 

    #!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --ntasks=1
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=24
#SBATCH --account=rcac
#SBATCH --qos=standby
#SBATCH --partition=cpu
#SBATCH --time=01:00:00
#SBATCH --job-name=evaluate
#SBATCH --array=1-4
#SBATCH --output=cluster-%x.%j.out
#SBATCH --error=cluster-%x.%j.err

module load biocontainers
module load bcftools/1.24
module load hap.py/0.3.9

# hap.py runs the vcfeval engine of RTG Tools (Java). Without a cap, the same task peaked between
# 1 and 39 GiB in different runs; RTG_MEM sets the memory that RTG Tools may use.
export RTG_MEM=8g

WORK=$SCRATCH/varcall-workshop
REF=$WORK/ref/GRCh38_no_alt.fa
SDF=$WORK/ref/GRCh38_no_alt.sdf
TRUTHDIR=$WORK/resources/truth
OUTDIR=$WORK/results/eval
mkdir -p $OUTDIR

# One sample and truth set per array task: task N reads line N+1 of truth_sets.tsv
LINE=$(sed -n "$((SLURM_ARRAY_TASK_ID + 1))p" $TRUTHDIR/truth_sets.tsv)
IFS=$'\t' read -r SAMPLE TRUTH TRUTH_VCF TRUTH_BED <<< "$LINE"

# Evaluate the calls before and after filtering
for CALLS in norm filtered; do
    # hap.py compares one sample: keep that sample's column and the sites where it has an ALT allele.
    # The file name includes the truth set: two tasks evaluate HG002 at the same time.
    bcftools view -s $SAMPLE -c 1 -Oz --write-index=tbi \
        -o $OUTDIR/$SAMPLE.$TRUTH.$CALLS.calls.vcf.gz $WORK/results/vcf/trio.$CALLS.vcf.gz

    # 24 cores for memory (about 1.9 GB each), 16 threads
    hap.py $TRUTHDIR/$TRUTH_VCF $OUTDIR/$SAMPLE.$TRUTH.$CALLS.calls.vcf.gz \
        -f $TRUTHDIR/$TRUTH_BED \
        -r $REF \
        -o $OUTDIR/$SAMPLE.$TRUTH.$CALLS \
        -l chr20 \
        --roc QUAL \
        --engine vcfeval \
        --engine-vcfeval-template $SDF \
        --threads 16
done

    The four array tasks are the four lines of resources/truth/truth_sets.tsv: task 1 is HG002 against benchmark v5.0q (NIST’s current release for HG002), task 2 HG002 against v4.2.1 (for comparison), and tasks 3 and 4 HG003 and HG004 against v4.2.1. Each task evaluates the calls twice, before filtering (trio.norm) and after (trio.filtered). In the workshop’s test runs each task took 1.5 to 2.5 minutes, plus the time waiting in the queue.

    In the workshop, submit task 1 only. --array=1 on the command line replaces the --array=1-4 of the script:

    BASH 

    cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/scripts
sbatch --array=1 evaluate.sh

    Then copy the results of the other three tasks from the completed results, so that Step 5 can compare all four:

    BASH 

    cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/eval/HG002.v4.2.1.* $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/eval/
cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/eval/HG003.v4.2.1.* $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/eval/
cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/eval/HG004.v4.2.1.* $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/eval/

    Working on your own, submit all four tasks instead:

    BASH 

    cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/scripts
sbatch evaluate.sh

    What the commands do:

    • bcftools view -s $SAMPLE -c 1: hap.py compares one sample with one benchmark, so we give it one sample’s column. -c 1 keeps only records where that sample carries at least one ALT allele; the trio file also has records where this sample is 0/0 or masked (./.), which are not calls for this sample.
    • -f $TRUTH_BED: the confident regions. hap.py counts query calls outside them as UNK (not assessed), not as false positives, so precision says nothing about calls outside the regions. Without -f, every call outside the benchmark’s knowledge would count against us. For example, HG002’s 1/1 call at chr20:29,070,822 in the centromere (FILTER HighDP;LowMQ) lies outside both HG002 benchmark regions, so in the evaluation of the unfiltered calls hap.py counts it as UNK, whether it is real or not.
    • -l chr20: compare chromosome 20 only. hap.py otherwise processes chr1-22, X and Y; with a whole-genome benchmark, every benchmark variant on another chromosome would become a false negative.
    • --engine vcfeval --engine-vcfeval-template $SDF: the haplotype-aware comparison, with the reference in the format it needs (ref/GRCh38_no_alt.sdf, prepared for the workshop).
    • --roc QUAL: also compute precision and recall at every QUAL threshold (Step 6).
    • 24 cores, 16 threads: hap.py’s memory use varies from run to run. In the workshop’s test runs the same task peaked anywhere between 1 and 39 GiB, more than the memory that comes with 16 cores, so the script requests 24 cores for their memory and runs 16 threads. The HG002 v5.0q task (task 1) peaked at 4.4 GiB in the latest test run and never above 10.2 GiB in five runs. The script also sets RTG_MEM, the memory setting of RTG Tools, whose vcfeval engine hap.py runs; whether it limits the peak has not been confirmed.
    Callout

    Short on time?

    If your evaluation job fails or is still waiting when we reach Step 5, copy the hap.py summaries and ROC tables from the results copy:

    BASH 

    cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/eval/*.summary.csv $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/eval/
cp /depot/workshop/data/varcall-workshop_results/results/eval/*.roc.Locations.*.csv.gz $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop/results/eval/

    Step 5: Read the hap.py summary

    When squeue -u $USER no longer lists the evaluate job, look at the results on the login node. column aligns the comma-separated fields, and cut -c1-120 keeps the lines on screen:

    BASH 

    cd $SCRATCH/varcall-workshop
ls results/eval/*.summary.csv
column -s, -t results/eval/HG002.v5.0q.norm.summary.csv | cut -c1-120

    OUTPUT 

    results/eval/HG002.v4.2.1.filtered.summary.csv
results/eval/HG002.v4.2.1.norm.summary.csv
results/eval/HG002.v5.0q.filtered.summary.csv
results/eval/HG002.v5.0q.norm.summary.csv
results/eval/HG003.v4.2.1.filtered.summary.csv
results/eval/HG003.v4.2.1.norm.summary.csv
results/eval/HG004.v4.2.1.filtered.summary.csv
results/eval/HG004.v4.2.1.norm.summary.csv
Type   Filter  TRUTH.TOTAL  TRUTH.TP  TRUTH.FN  QUERY.TOTAL  QUERY.FP  QUERY.UNK  FP.gt  METRIC.Recall  METRIC.Precision
INDEL  ALL     18173        15261     2912      20265        2245      2731       1737   0.839762       0.871963
INDEL  PASS    18173        15261     2912      20265        2245      2731       1737   0.839762       0.871963
SNP    ALL     75854        74963     891       119754       1570      43202      286    0.988254       0.979491
SNP    PASS    75854        74963     891       119754       1570      43202      286    0.988254       0.979491

    Each row is one variant type (INDEL, SNP) and one set of calls: ALL counts every call, PASS only calls with PASS in FILTER. Before filtering there is no FILTER label, so the two rows are the same. The columns (hap.py documentation):

    Column Meaning
    TRUTH.TOTAL benchmark variants in the confident regions
    TRUTH.TP, TRUTH.FN benchmark variants we found, and missed
    QUERY.TOTAL our calls for HG002
    QUERY.FP our calls inside the confident regions that the benchmark does not support
    QUERY.UNK our calls outside the confident regions: not assessed
    FP.gt false positives where the variant is right but the genotype is wrong
    METRIC.Recall, METRIC.Precision as defined above

    METRIC.F1_Score is further to the right, past the 120 characters shown. For the unfiltered calls against v5.0q, SNV recall and precision are 0.9883 and 0.9795, and indel 0.8398 and 0.8720: indels are much harder.

    Now the filtered calls:

    BASH 

    column -s, -t results/eval/HG002.v5.0q.filtered.summary.csv | cut -c1-120

    OUTPUT 

    Type   Filter  TRUTH.TOTAL  TRUTH.TP  TRUTH.FN  QUERY.TOTAL  QUERY.FP  QUERY.UNK  FP.gt  METRIC.Recall  METRIC.Precision
INDEL  ALL     18173        14248     3925      17615        1133      2213       782    0.78402        0.926438
INDEL  PASS    18173        14161     4012      16823        1060      1575       768    0.779233       0.930483
SNP    ALL     75854        74596     1258      114284       1065      38614      173    0.983416       0.985926
SNP    PASS    75854        74383     1471      96848        848       21609      159    0.980607       0.988729

    The PASS rows are the frozen values of this workshop: SNV recall 0.980607 and precision 0.988729, indel recall 0.779233 and precision 0.930483.

    The figure puts both summaries and the ROC tables of Step 6 on one plot. Each curve shows the unfiltered calls filtered at every possible QUAL threshold: high thresholds sit at the left (few calls kept, low recall), no threshold at the right end. The two points are the PASS rows above.

    Two filters, two effects

    The filtered file differs from the unfiltered one in two ways, and the summary separates them:

    • the ALL row of the filtered file counts every record, whatever its FILTER label, but with the genotype mask applied (masked genotypes are gone, because -c 1 drops ./.);
    • the PASS row adds the site filters.

    So unfiltered ALL against filtered ALL shows the genotype mask alone, and filtered ALL against filtered PASS shows the site filters. The reference run, against v4.2.1 (comparison benchmark; reference-run memo, section 4):

    Type Raw: recall / precision After the genotype mask After the site filters too
    SNV 0.9948 / 0.9862 0.9931 / 0.9891 0.9907 / 0.9914
    Indel 0.9432 / 0.9465 0.9080 / 0.9712 0.9063 / 0.9727

    For SNVs, both steps trade a little recall for precision. For indels, the genotype mask causes almost all of the recall loss and most of the precision gain: indel genotypes with GQ below 20 are common, and when the mask sets a real but uncertain genotype to missing, a true positive becomes a false negative. That is the precision-recall trade-off: any threshold that removes more wrong calls also removes some right ones, and where the balance should sit depends on what the calls are for. A screen for candidate variants that a person will check by hand can favor recall; a call set that goes straight into a report needs precision.

    Challenge

    Challenge: the trade-off in your own summary

    Using the two v5.0q summaries you printed (unfiltered and filtered):

    1. For indels, write down recall and precision for unfiltered ALL, filtered ALL and filtered PASS. Which step costs the most recall?
    2. Look at FP.gt for indels and SNVs in the filtered PASS rows. What fraction of the false positives are genotype errors in each type?
    3. Why can a QUAL threshold do little about those genotype errors?
    1. Indels against v5.0q, recall / precision: unfiltered ALL 0.8398 / 0.8720; filtered ALL (genotype mask) 0.7840 / 0.9264; filtered PASS (mask and site filters) 0.7792 / 0.9305. The mask costs 0.056 of recall, the site filters 0.005 more. As against v4.2.1, the genotype mask causes most of the indel recall loss.
    2. Indels: 768 of 1,060 false positives are genotype errors (72%). SNVs: 159 of 848 (19%). Most indel false positives are real variant sites called with the wrong genotype; most SNV false positives are not.
    3. QUAL measures how sure the caller is that the site is variant at all. A genotype error is at a real variant site, which can have a high QUAL; only the genotype is wrong. QUAL cannot tell the two genotypes apart, so a QUAL threshold removes these false positives no faster than the true positives around them.

    Step 6: Predict, then test a threshold

    --roc QUAL made hap.py compute recall and precision at every QUAL value of the unfiltered calls, as if we had filtered at that value. The tables are in results/eval/HG002.v5.0q.norm.roc.Locations.SNP.csv.gz and ...INDEL.csv.gz.

    Challenge

    Challenge: predict, then test a QUAL threshold

    Our filter flags QUAL below 30. Suppose we raised the threshold to 225.

    1. Predict, before looking: what happens to SNV recall and precision? To indel recall and precision? Which type changes more?
    2. Test the prediction. Each command prints the rows of the ROC table at the first QUAL values at or above 30 and 225, with the columns QUAL, recall, precision and F1:

    BASH 

    zcat results/eval/HG002.v5.0q.norm.roc.Locations.SNP.csv.gz | tail -n +2 | cut -d, -f7,8,9,11 | sort -t, -k1,1g | awk -F, '(30 <= $1 && !a++) || (225 <= $1 && !b++)'
zcat results/eval/HG002.v5.0q.norm.roc.Locations.INDEL.csv.gz | tail -n +2 | cut -d, -f7,8,9,11 | sort -t, -k1,1g | awk -F, '(30 <= $1 && !a++) || (225 <= $1 && !b++)'

    OUTPUT 

    30.481899,0.987067,0.984282,0.985673
225.110992,0.977404,0.993196,0.985237
30.222500,0.834095,0.877202,0.855105
225.104996,0.748638,0.902337,0.818333

    The first two lines are SNVs, the last two indels. From QUAL 30 to 225 against v5.0q, SNV recall falls from 0.9871 to 0.9774 and precision rises from 0.9843 to 0.9932; indel recall falls from 0.8341 to 0.7486 and precision rises from 0.8772 to 0.9023. Indel recall falls much more. Indel precision rises more in absolute terms, but look at the wrong calls, 1 minus precision: for SNVs they fall from 1.6% to 0.7% of calls, by more than half; for indels from 12.3% to 9.8%, by about a fifth. Most indel false positives are genotype errors, which QUAL does not separate (previous challenge). Against v4.2.1 the reference run shows the same pattern: from QUAL 30 to 225, SNV recall 0.9944 to 0.9906 and precision 0.9889 to 0.9949; indel recall 0.9425 to 0.9074, precision 0.9478 to 0.9511.

    Callout

    Do not tune thresholds on the benchmark

    The ROC table makes it tempting to pick the QUAL with the best F1. In your SNV table against v5.0q, F1 peaks at QUAL 117.7 (F1 0.9869). Against v4.2.1, the same calls peak at about QUAL 156-160 (F1 0.9931 in the reference run). The best threshold moved because the test set changed, not the calls. Choosing it for that reason would be tuning on the test set: the threshold would be fitted to this benchmark, these samples and this region, and the scores would then overstate how well it works anywhere else. Choose thresholds from the call set’s own distributions and from conventions, as in Step 2, and use the benchmark only to measure the result. On your own data there will usually be no benchmark at all.

    Same calls, two benchmarks

    Look at the HG002 summary against the older benchmark:

    BASH 

    column -s, -t results/eval/HG002.v4.2.1.filtered.summary.csv | cut -c1-120

    OUTPUT 

    Type   Filter  TRUTH.TOTAL  TRUTH.TP  TRUTH.FN  QUERY.TOTAL  QUERY.FP  QUERY.UNK  FP.gt  METRIC.Recall  METRIC.Precision
INDEL  ALL     11256        10221     1035      17615        302       7123       241    0.908049       0.971216
INDEL  PASS    11256        10201     1055      16823        286       6364       239    0.906272       0.972655
SNP    ALL     71333        70839     494       114284       778       42598      40     0.993075       0.989147
SNP    PASS    71333        70671     662       96848        613       25496      32     0.99072        0.991409

    The calls are identical, but PASS indel recall is 0.7792 against v5.0q and 0.9063 against v4.2.1, and SNV recall 0.9806 against 0.9907. The benchmark defines the score. NIST built v5.0q from a complete diploid assembly of HG002 (the T2T HG002 Q100 assembly), which “allows for the characterization and inclusion of challenging genomic regions and variant types previously excluded from GIAB benchmark sets”, including segmental duplications and large tandem repeats (v5.0q README). On chromosome 20 its confident regions cover 58.1 Mb against 56.9 Mb, and it holds 6% more SNVs and 61% more indels than v4.2.1 (reference-run memo). The variants it adds sit in harder sequence, where short reads struggle, so recall falls. The README also says that some regions in v4.2.1 are excluded from v5.0q, for example regions inside inversions, and that results “should be carefully evaluated” because the approach is new.

    Discussion

    Discussion: which number would you report?

    A paper reports “indel recall 0.91 against GIAB HG002”. Another reports 0.78. Could both describe the same pipeline? What would you need to know before comparing them? What should you write when you report your own accuracy?

    Challenge

    Challenge: same calls, two benchmarks (self-paced)

    1. From the two filtered HG002 summaries, compare TRUTH.TOTAL for SNVs and indels. How many more benchmark variants does v5.0q contain?
    2. Compare QUERY.UNK. Why is it smaller against v5.0q?
    3. Which part of the drop in indel recall comes from variants the newer benchmark adds, and which from calls that changed? (Hint: did any call change?)
    1. v5.0q: 75,854 SNVs and 18,173 indels; v4.2.1: 71,333 and 11,256. That is 6% more SNVs and 61% more indels.
    2. QUERY.UNK counts our calls outside the confident regions. v5.0q’s regions cover more of chromosome 20 and more of the difficult sequence, so more of our calls are assessed (and more of them can turn out to be false positives).
    3. All of it comes from the benchmark: the calls are the same file. The added benchmark variants lie mostly in harder sequence, where our calls miss more of them.

    Difficult regions and stratification

    Accuracy is not uniform along the genome. Homopolymers and tandem repeats make indels hard to align and to represent; segmental duplications and regions of low mappability attract reads from elsewhere; the centromere combines all of these. GIAB publishes stratification BED files that divide the genome into such contexts, and hap.py can report precision and recall for each of them (Krusche et al. 2019). They are not part of the workshop copy, so we do not compute per-context numbers here; the Ts/Tv inside and outside the benchmark regions, and in the centromere, gave a first view of the same effect.

    Proxy measures when there is no truth set

    For your own samples there is usually no benchmark. These measures still tell you something:

    • Ts/Tv, as above: before and after filtering, inside and outside regions you trust, across samples. A ratio far below that of the known variation of your organism points to errors.
    • Mendelian consistency in families: a child’s genotype must be explainable by one allele from each parent. In Episode 8 we count the sites where it is not.
    • Replicate concordance: the same sample sequenced twice should give the same calls; disagreements point to errors.
    • Known sites: the fraction of your calls already listed in a population database (for example gnomAD, Episode 7). An unusually low fraction suggests errors, although real rare variants are often absent from such databases.

    None of these gives precision and recall, and each can be fooled, but together they show whether a filter moves a call set in the right direction.

    Common problems

    Symptom Likely cause Fix
    a filter flags far too many or too few sites INFO/DP and FMT/DP confused: one is summed over samples, the other per sample name the field explicitly (INFO/DP, FMT/DP)
    the filter keeps what it should remove -i and -e swapped -e names what fails, -i what passes
    records disappeared after filtering a hard filter: -e without -s add -s NAME to label instead of delete
    precision far too low hap.py run without the confident-region BED (-f) give -f the benchmark BED
    recall close to 0, or hap.py complains about samples a multi-sample VCF given to hap.py, or the wrong sample extract one sample with bcftools view -s SAMPLE -c 1
    recall far too low whole-genome benchmark without -l restrict with -l chr20
    counts that differ between tools calls not normalized bcftools norm -f ref.fa -m -any (Episode 5A)

    Summary

    Key Points
    • bcftools stats and simple percentiles of QUAL, depth and MQ show the tails that filters should target; Ts/Tv rises when errors are removed.
    • Thresholds come from the call set’s distributions and from conventions; tuning them on the benchmark is test-set leakage.
    • Site filters (-s with QUAL, INFO/DP, INFO/MQ) label records in FILTER and keep them; the genotype mask (-S . with FMT/DP, FMT/GQ) sets single genotypes to missing.
    • hap.py with vcfeval compares one sample’s calls with a benchmark inside its confident regions; calls outside them are UNK, not scored.
    • Precision and recall trade against each other: the genotype mask raises indel precision and costs indel recall.
    • The benchmark defines the score: the same calls score lower against the more complete v5.0q.
    • Without a truth set, use proxies: Ts/Tv, Mendelian consistency, replicate concordance and known sites.
